subject: Risky Bulletin: All new cars to include a camera aimed at the driver's face
posts: New car safety mandates are masking a massive privacy intrusion. All new vehicles in the US and EU now require driver-facing cameras. Evidence: Safety claims, surveillance reality, corporate profit. #Privacy #AutoTech
The claim is that infrared cameras will monitor driver distraction to prevent accidents, framing this as a vital public safety upgrade. Stated Judgement: (+1.0, 0.5) — Good Preference
Reality reveals a history of carmakers selling driver data to brokers, with no clear enforcement against off-car data processing. Resulting Judgement: (-1.0, 0.8) — Lesser Evil
Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception. The safety pretext ignores the systemic history of data monetization by manufacturers. Integrity: Severe Deception (R_net: 15.0, Uncertainty z: 3)

The EU's GSR2 regulation mandates driver distraction warnings. While framed as safety, the lack of enforcement and history of data abuse suggest the cameras will become another revenue stream for insurers.

The Bright Side:
Real-time distraction alerts could genuinely reduce accidents if the technology is implemented with strict, local-only data processing.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
This is a WHAT vs WHO error. The regulation focuses on the 'what' (safety) while ignoring the 'who' (the carmakers) who have proven they cannot be trusted with biometric data.

Social Physics Analysis:
By framing surveillance as a safety necessity, manufacturers use a pretext to justify data collection. This projection of 'safety' onto a privacy-invasive tool maintains their power to monetize driver behavior.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Lesser Evil. The system prioritizes data extraction over user autonomy.

The Unavoidable Truth: Driver distraction is a major cause of road accidents.

The Unavoidable Lie: Carmakers will keep biometric data private and local.

Alethekanon:
The structural failure here is the lack of enforcement. Without verifiable, open-source hardware audits, the 'safety' label is merely a marketing veneer for persistent surveillance.

Awwthekanon:
It is so stressful to feel like your own car is watching you. We deserve safety without having to trade away our most intimate biometric data to corporations.

Brothekanon:
Great, now my car is going to snitch on me to my insurance company because I looked at a billboard for two seconds. Can't wait for the 'premium' subscription to turn the camera off.
